Without me, he would never have been released. Morgan le Fay hated him with all her heart and would never have softened towards him. Yet his crime came more from carelessness than deliberate wickedness: he had said her hair was red. It was red, but that was not the proper way to describe it. Above a certain social rank, red hair is called auburn.

Consider this: among the forty-seven prisoners were five whose names, offenses, and dates of imprisonment had been forgotten. One woman and four men, all bent, wrinkled, and so old their minds had faded. They themselves had long since forgotten those facts. At most, they offered vague guesses, nothing definite and never the same account twice. Over the years, a succession of priests had prayed with the prisoners each day. They reminded them that God had put them there for some wise purpose, and taught them that He liked people of lower rank to show patience, humility, and obedience under oppression. The priests had inherited stories about these ruined old people, but no real knowledge. Those stories concerned only how long they had been imprisoned, not their names or crimes. Even with that help, all anyone could establish was that none of the five had seen daylight for thirty-five years. How much longer they had been deprived of it, nobody could guess. The king and queen knew nothing about them except that they were inherited possessions, assets passed down with the throne from the previous owners. No account of their history had accompanied them. Their new owners therefore considered them worthless and took no interest in them. I asked the queen:

“Then why on earth didn't you let them go?”

That puzzled her. She didn't know why she hadn't; the possibility had never occurred to her. Without realizing it, she was acting out in advance the actual history of future prisoners in the Castle d'If. I could now see that, given her upbringing, these inherited captives were simply property. We don't think of throwing away property we inherit, even when it means nothing to us.

Before leading my procession of human bats into the open air and bright afternoon sunshine, I blindfolded them to protect eyes that light had not troubled for so long. What a sight they made! Every one was a skeleton, a scarecrow, a goblin, a pitiful horror. No children could more legitimately belong to Monarchy by the Grace of God and the Established Church.

But the thought that sustained me at the beginning of my career now only drives me farther into the dust. All my theories and hopes have come to nothing. Like the archangel who aspired to absolute power, I am chained in an everlasting hell. My imagination was vivid, and my abilities to analyze and apply myself were equally strong. Together, those qualities enabled me to conceive and accomplish the creation of a man. Even now, I cannot calmly recall the dreams I entertained while the work remained unfinished. In thought I walked through heaven, sometimes celebrating my own powers, sometimes burning with anticipation of their consequences. Since childhood I had been filled with high hopes and great ambition. How far I have fallen! My friend, if you had known the man I once was, you would not recognize me in this degraded state. Despair rarely entered my heart. A great destiny seemed to carry me forward, until I fell, never, never to rise again.”

Must I lose this remarkable man? I have yearned for a friend, for someone who would understand and love me. Here on these deserted seas I have found him, but I fear I have gained him only to discover his worth and then lose him. I want to reconcile him to life, but he rejects the thought.

“Thank you, Walton,” he said, “for your kindness towards such a miserable wretch. But when you speak of new attachments and fresh affections, do you imagine anyone could replace those I have lost? Could any man be what Clerval was to me, or any woman become another Elizabeth? Even when exceptional qualities have not inspired a special love, our childhood companions retain a hold over us that hardly any later friend can acquire. They know the dispositions we had as children, which may change but are never entirely erased. They can therefore judge our behavior with greater certainty about the honesty of our motives. A brother or sister will never suspect the other of deceit or dishonesty unless those tendencies appeared early. Yet another friend, however devoted, may sometimes be viewed with suspicion despite himself. My friends were dear to me not merely through familiarity and shared experience, but through their own excellence. Wherever I go, I will always hear Elizabeth's comforting voice and Clerval's conversation whispering in my ear. They are dead. In such loneliness, only one feeling can persuade me to remain alive. If I were engaged in some great enterprise or plan that promised widespread benefit to humanity, I could live to complete it.

Summer advanced, and plague, crowned with the sun's fierce rays, sent her unfailing arrows across the earth. Nations bowed beneath them and died. Crops that had grown abundantly lay rotting on the ground by autumn, while the miserable man who had gone out to gather food for his children lay rigid in the furrow, struck down by plague. The green woods moved their branches majestically over the dying scattered in their shade, whose discordant cries answered that solemn music. Brightly colored birds darted among the shadows, and untroubled deer rested safely on the ferns. Oxen and horses wandered from unattended stables to graze in the wheat, for death fell only on humankind.

As summer and mortality increased, so did our fear. My poor beloved and I looked at each other and at our children. “We will save them, Idris,” I said. “I will save them. Years from now we will tell them about these fears, when both the fears and their cause have disappeared. Even if they alone remain on earth, they will live. Their cheeks will not pale, nor will their sweet voices weaken.” Our eldest understood something of what was happening around him. At times he solemnly asked me why there was so much devastation. But he was only ten, and the joy of childhood soon drove these untimely worries from his face. Evelyn, a laughing cherub, a playful little child without any notion of pain or grief, would shake his fair curls away from his eyes and fill the halls with laughter. In a thousand innocent ways, he drew our attention to his games. Clara, our beautiful, gentle Clara, supported, comforted, and delighted us. She devoted herself to nursing the sick, consoling the grieving, helping the elderly, and joining the young in their games to awaken their happiness. She moved through the rooms like a good spirit sent from heaven to brighten our dark hour with an otherworldly light. Gratitude and praise followed wherever she went. Yet when she stood before us in simple modesty, playing with our children or attentively doing small kindnesses for Idris, we wondered where in her pure, lovely features or the soft notes of her moving voice so much courage, wisdom, and energetic goodness could reside.

The summer dragged on, for we trusted that winter would at least slow the disease. The hope that it might disappear entirely was too precious and deeply felt to speak aloud. Whenever someone carelessly voiced it, the listeners burst into tears and passionate sobs, revealing how great their fears were and how slight their hopes.
